Part 1

Derive the formula for the confidence interval for a difference of means assuming independent samples and equal population variances. You may assume the formula for the pivotal statistic.

To derive this formula for the confidence interval for a differences of means using the given assumptions we can define our pivotal statistic as:1

\[ T = \frac{(\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2}) - (\mu_1-\mu_2)}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}} \]

From here we can define our probability statement:

\[ P\left(-t_{\alpha/2,\nu} \le T \le t_{\alpha/2,\nu}\right) = 1- \alpha \]

Then we can substitute in \(T\) and \(\nu = n_1+n_2-2\) and solve for our parameter of interest which is \((\mu_1 - \mu_2)\):

\[ P\left(-t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \le \frac{(\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2}) - (\mu_1-\mu_2)}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}} \le t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2}\right) = 1- \alpha \]

\[ P\left(-t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \le (\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2}) - (\mu_1-\mu_2) \le t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2})\cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \right) = 1- \alpha \]

\[ P\left(-(\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})-t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \le - (\mu_1-\mu_2) \le -(\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})+t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2})\cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \right) = 1- \alpha \]

\[ P\left((\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})+t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \ge (\mu_1-\mu_2) \ge (\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})-t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2})\cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \right) = 1- \alpha \]

Therefore we have:

\[ P\left((\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})-t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \le (\mu_1-\mu_2) \le (\bar{Y_1} - \bar{Y_2})+t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2})\cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \right) = 1- \alpha \]

And the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \((\mu_1-\mu_2)\) is:

\[ (\bar{Y}_1-\bar{Y}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \]

Handwritten Work

Part 2

The final formula for the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \((\mu_1-\mu_2)\) is:

\[ (\bar{Y}_1-\bar{Y}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,n_1+n_2-2} \cdot S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}} \]

Part 3

Make an R function (you may use t.test()) that will create 3 boxplots (one per category: “Text line”, “Witness line” and “Intersection”) on the one graphical interface and also print a list of all possible confidence intervals. I will assume \(\alpha = 0.05\).

# Define the function
mp_13 <- function(df, vareq){
  
  # Make the boxplot of the data
  boxplot(df, 
        main = "Comparison of Text, Witness, and Intersection",
        ylab = "Values")

 # Identify all possible pairwise combinations of the column names
  group_names <- names(df)
  combos <- combn(group_names, 2)

  # Calculate confidence intervals
  l <- lapply(1:ncol(combos), function(i) {
    g1 <- combos[1, i]
    g2 <- combos[2, i]
    
    # t.test with 95% CI (alpha = 0.05) - using column name pairs
    test_result <- t.test(df[[g1]], df[[g2]], var.equal = vareq)
    
    # Return the confidence interval
    return(test_result$conf.int)
  })

  # Name the list elements 
  names(l) <- paste(combos[1, ], "vs", combos[2, ])
  
  # Return final named list
  return(l)
}

Use the function on the given dataset where vareq = TRUE:

# Use given data
mp_13(zinc, vareq=TRUE)

## $`Text vs Witness`
## [1] -0.07229773  0.22996440
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95
## 
## $`Text vs Intersection`
## [1] -0.03075723  0.13875723
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95
## 
## $`Witness vs Intersection`
## [1] -0.13613439  0.08646773
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95

Part 4

Based on a visual inspection of the boxplots, the assumption of equal variance does not appear to be justified. While the Text and Intersection lines show a relatively similar spread, the Witness line is clearly distinct with a much larger and more stretched-out IQR. Furthermore, the whiskers for the Witness line differ in length slightly from the other two. Additionally, each line category has a small sample size, which can lead to unreliable results when running tests like var.test() (F-test) in R to determine if this assumption holds.

Part 5

To do the Welch’s test we can use our function from Part 3 and set vareq = FALSE:

# Run again with unequal variances
mp_13(zinc, vareq = FALSE)

## $`Text vs Witness`
## [1] -0.0436211  0.2012878
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95
## 
## $`Text vs Intersection`
## [1] -0.05064814  0.15864814
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95
## 
## $`Witness vs Intersection`
## [1] -0.1332283  0.0835616
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95

Based on the zinc measurements provided, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the ink at the Text line and the Witness line are different. The physicist’s beam might show different averages, but the overlap is too great to prove tampering “beyond a reasonable doubt.” Intel’s accusation against the inventor is not statistically supported by this specific zinc data.
